entry: Spanish conquistador. Born in Trujillo, Spain, to a poor family, he sailed to the [[New World]] in 1509 and in 1513 joined an expedition across the Isthmus of Panama, where his party became the first Europeans to see the [[Pacific Ocean]] from the Americas. He later served as mayor of [[Panama City]] and made two failed expeditions to [[Peru]] before the Crown of Castile authorized a campaign of conquest in 1529. In November 1532 he captured the Inca emperor [[Atahualpa]] at the Battle of Cajamarca. Atahualpa filled a room with gold as ransom, but was executed by garrotting in July 1533. Pizarro then entered [[Cusco|Cuzco]], the Inca capital, and founded [[Lima]] in January 1535. The Crown of Castile made him 1st Marquess of the Conquest in 1537. He was assassinated amid political power struggles.

Highly radioactive [[Alkali metal|alkali metal]] with atomic number 87 and symbol Fr. Its most stable isotope, francium-223, has a half-life of only 22 minutes, and its isotopes decay quickly into [[Astatine|astatine]], [[Radium|radium]] and [[Radon|radon]]. It is the second-most electropositive element, behind only [[Caesium|caesium]], and the second rarest naturally occurring element after astatine. Marguerite Perey discovered it in France on January 7, 1939; the element is named after France. It was the last element first discovered in nature rather than by synthesis. Trace amounts occur in [[Uranium|uranium]] ores, and as little as 1 ounce (28 g) exists at any time in the [[Earth's crust|Earth's crust]]. Bulk francium has never been seen, and the largest laboratory sample was a cluster of more than 300,000 atoms.

Conflict between [[France]] and the Prussia-led North German Confederation, 1870–71. [[Otto von Bismarck]] published an altered version of the Ems dispatch, reporting the Prussian king's rejection of a French demand, and it inflamed opinion in [[Paris]]. Some historians argue that Bismarck deliberately provoked the war to draw the southern German states into the Confederation; others contend he exploited events as they unfolded. Superior in numbers, training, leadership and use of railways and artillery, German forces won a series of victories, culminating at Sedan, where [[Napoleon III]] was captured. Paris was besieged and fell on January 28, 1871. The Treaty of Frankfurt (May 10, 1871) gave Germany billions of francs in indemnity and most of [[Alsace]] and parts of Lorraine. The war hastened the proclamation of the [[German Empire]] under [[Wilhelm I]] and ended imperial rule in France, though resentment over the war's aftermath triggered the [[Paris Commune]].

Regime led by [[Francisco Franco|Franco]] that ruled Nationalist-held Spain from 1936 and all of Spain from 1939 until 1975. It was a one-party authoritarian dictatorship centered on Franco and the Movimiento Nacional, and it emerged from the [[Spanish Civil War]]. Historians debate whether it was fascist, since it shared fascist features early on but later became more conventionally authoritarian. Spain stayed formally neutral in World War II while supporting the [[Axis powers]] in practice. In the 1950s it moved toward economic liberalization, and a transition to democracy began after Franco's death.

American security consultant and former con man. His 1980 autobiography, *Catch Me If You Can*, claimed that as a teenager he impersonated a [[Pan Am|Pan American World Airways]] pilot, physician and lawyer while passing millions of dollars in fraudulent checks. Investigations beginning in 1978 found no evidence for most of these claims, and records show he was imprisoned for much of the period. Documented offenses include check fraud and a federal case involving ten forged Pan Am checks totaling less than $1,500. The book inspired a 2002 film directed by [[Steven Spielberg]].

Italian-born American film director, producer and screenwriter. Born in Bisacquino, near [[Palermo]], [[Sicily]], he was raised in [[Los Angeles]] and studied [[Chemical engineering|chemical engineering]] at the California Institute of Technology. He was one of America's most influential directors during the 1930s, winning three [[Academy Awards]] for Best Director from six nominations, for films including *It Happened One Night* (1934), *Mr. Deeds Goes to Town* (1936) and *You Can't Take It with You* (1938). During [[World War II]] he served in the U.S. Army Signal Corps and produced the *Why We Fight* propaganda series. His later films, including *It's a Wonderful Life* (1946), performed poorly on release, and he retired from filmmaking in the mid-1960s. Critics later reevaluated his films favorably. He served as president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

Italian-American mobster, boss of the [[Lucky Luciano|Luciano]] crime family in [[New York City]]. Born in [[Calabria]], Italy, he worked with Lucky Luciano in Prohibition-era bootlegging and became boss in 1938. His televised testimony at the 1951 Kefauver Committee hearings brought nationwide attention to organized crime. In 1957 [[Vincent Gigante]] shot him outside his [[Manhattan]] apartment on the orders of Vito Genovese, but the bullet only grazed his head. He then retired, and Genovese succeeded him as boss.

Canadian-American architect and designer. Born Goldberg in [[Toronto]], he changed his surname to Gehry in 1954 after his wife expressed concern about [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]], and he graduated from the University of Southern California's School of Architecture that year. He rose to prominence in the 1970s with a style that blended everyday materials such as corrugated steel and chain-link fencing into complex, dynamic forms. His buildings, characterized by sculptural, often undulating exteriors, include the Guggenheim Museum in [[Bilbao]], Spain, the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles and the Louis Vuitton Foundation in Paris. Their innovative materials include [[Titanium|titanium]] and [[Stainless steel|stainless steel]]. His approach was described as deconstructivist, though he resisted categorization. He received the 1989 Pritzker Architecture Prize, considered the field's highest honor.

American science-fiction author. Best known for the novel *Dune* (1965) and its five sequels, among the best-selling [[Science fiction|science fiction]] novels of all time. Herbert also worked as a newspaper journalist, photographer, book reviewer and ecological consultant. Born in Tacoma, Washington, he served in the U.S. Navy during [[World War II]] until a head injury led to a medical discharge. [[David Lynch]] adapted *Dune* for film in 1984, and Denis Villeneuve adapted it again in 2021.

American architect, designer, writer and educator. He designed more than 1,000 structures over a creative period of 70 years and pioneered organic architecture, a philosophy of designing in harmony with humanity and the environment. Raised in [[Wisconsin]], he studied civil engineering at the University of Wisconsin, then apprenticed in Chicago with [[Louis Sullivan]] and opened his own practice there in 1893. Wright played a key role in the architectural movements of the twentieth century, pioneering the Prairie School and developing the Usonian home concept. [[Fallingwater]] (1935) has been called "the best all-time work of American architecture". His Taliesin Fellowship mentored hundreds of apprentices. In 1991 the American Institute of Architects called him "the greatest American architect of all time", and in 2019 a selection of his work became a [[World Heritage Site]].

American drug trafficker active in Harlem in the late 1960s and early 1970s. He cut out middlemen by buying [[Heroin|heroin]] directly from the Golden Triangle in Southeast Asia. Lucas claimed he smuggled it in the coffins of dead American servicemen, a claim denied by his associate Leslie "Ike" Atkinson. Convicted in 1976 and sentenced to 70 years, he became an informant and entered the Witness Protection Program. His sentences were reduced in 1981 to time served plus lifetime parole. The 2007 film *American Gangster* fictionalized aspects of his life.

American singer and songwriter. Credited by several critics as a pioneer of alternative R&B, he began as a ghostwriter and in 2010 joined the [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] collective Odd Future. His debut studio [[Album|album]], *Channel Orange* (2012), won a [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] for Best Urban Contemporary Album. His second album, *Blonde* (2016), debuted atop the U.S. Billboard 200. After 2017 he released sporadic singles, worked as a photographer for magazines and launched the fashion brand Homer. He has sold over 2 million albums worldwide.

American singer and actor, regarded as one of the most influential entertainers of the 20th century. Born to Italian immigrants in Hoboken, New Jersey, he joined the Harry James band as a vocalist in 1939 and signed with [[Columbia Records]] four years later. His debut album, *The Voice of Frank Sinatra*, was released in 1946. At Capitol Records he recorded albums arranged by Nelson Riddle, including *In the Wee Small Hours* (1955), and in 1960 he founded Reprise Records. He recorded *Francis A. & Edward K.* with [[Duke Ellington]] in 1968. He won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for *From Here to Eternity* (1953). An estimated 150 million records have been sold worldwide.

American voice actor and former stand-up comedian. Beginning in the 1960s, he built a career with about 850 film, television and video game credits as of 2020. He voiced Fred Jones in *Scooby-Doo* from 1969 and Scooby-Doo himself from 2002, and he voiced Megatron and Soundwave in *Transformers*. He has voiced Garfield since 2007 and several characters in [[Matt Groening]]'s *Futurama*, including Nibbler. In 2016 he received a Lifetime Achievement Emmy Award.

American musician, satirist and filmmaker. Born in [[Baltimore]], Zappa composed rock, jazz, orchestral and [[Classical music|classical]] works and produced nearly all of his 60-plus albums. His music is marked by satire, improvisation and nonconformity. His debut album with the Mothers of Invention, *Freak Out!* (1966), paired satirical rock songs with extended sound collages. A strong advocate of [[Freedom of speech|freedom of speech]] and opponent of censorship, he was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1995, posthumously.

1931 American pre-Code [[Horror film|horror film]] directed by James Whale. Colin Clive starred as the scientist Henry Frankenstein, and [[Boris Karloff|Karloff]] played the creature. The film was produced and distributed by [[Universal Pictures]], and it was a commercial success. Adapted from a 1927 play that was itself based on [[Mary Shelley]]'s 1818 novel, it spawned sequels and spin-offs. Jack Pierce's makeup for the monster became iconic. In 1991 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry.

Gothic novel *Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus* by English author [[Mary Shelley]], first published anonymously in London on January 1, 1818. It tells of Victor Frankenstein, a young scientist who creates a sapient creature from body parts in an unorthodox experiment. Victor had been obsessed with [[Alchemy|alchemy]] in his youth. The story grew from a ghost-story challenge proposed by [[Lord Byron]] in 1816. The creature learns to read, including *[[Paradise Lost]]*, and takes vengeance on its creator. A revised edition published under Shelley's name appeared in 1831. Infused with Gothic and Romantic elements, it became one of the best-known works of English literature, spawning a complete genre of horror stories, films and plays, including the [[Frankenstein (1931 film)|1931 film]]. Popular usage often applies the name Frankenstein to the creature rather than its creator.

Most populous city in the German state of [[Hesse|Hesse]] (pop., 2025: 778,589). Frankfurt was first mentioned in 794 and was a free city for nearly five centuries and one of the most important cities of the [[Holy Roman Empire]]. It was annexed by [[Kingdom of Prussia|Prussia]] after the [[Austro-Prussian War]] in 1866 and has been part of Hesse since 1945. Frankfurt is one of the four institutional seats of the [[European Union]], home to the European Central Bank. Frankfurt Airport is Germany's busiest and the primary hub of [[Lufthansa]], and the city is a major financial center with the Frankfurt Stock Exchange and Deutsche Bank. Its skyscrapers have earned it the nickname Mainhattan.

32nd president of the United States, serving from 1933 until his death. Roosevelt graduated from [[Harvard University]] and was elected governor of New York before defeating [[Herbert Hoover]] in the 1932 presidential election. His first two terms centered on the [[Great Depression]], with the [[New Deal]] creating programs including the Securities and Exchange Commission and Social Security. He was the only president to serve more than two terms, winning re-election in 1936, 1940 and 1944. After the [[Attack on Pearl Harbor]], he obtained a declaration of war on Japan, then on Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy, and initiated development of the first atomic bomb. He helped lay the groundwork for the [[United Nations]]. His ordering of the [[Internment of Japanese Americans|internment of Japanese Americans]] has been criticized, but historical rankings consistently place him among the three greatest American presidents.

Western European people of Germanic origin, originally tribes near the lower [[Rhine]]. From the 3rd century Frankish tribes raided and settled across the Roman frontier, and Roman authorities later recruited large numbers of Franks as soldiers. In 406 the Franks tried to defend the border against an invasion by Alans and [[Vandals]]. In 451 Frankish groups fought on both sides at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains, where [[Attila]] was defeated. By the early 6th century [[Clovis I]], founder of the Merovingian dynasty, had united the whole of Gaul north of the Loire under Frankish rule. In 800 the pope crowned [[Charlemagne]] emperor of Western Europe. The Frankish realm was divided in 870 into the predecessors of the Kingdom of France and the [[Holy Roman Empire]]. The term Franks later came to denote Western Europeans generally, especially in the [[Crusades]].

[[Martinique|Martinique]]-born French psychiatrist and political philosopher. Fanon worked at a psychiatric hospital in [[Algeria]] and supported the [[Algerian War]] of independence from France, joining the Algerian National Liberation Front. His work on the psychological effects of [[Colonialism|colonialism]] made him a central figure in post-colonial studies. *Black Skin, White Masks* (1952) examined the internalized inferiority of colonized people, and *The Wretched of the Earth* (1961), prefaced by [[Jean-Paul Sartre]], argued for violence as a liberating force, a view both praised and criticized. Fanon also helped found institutional psychotherapy and argued that many [[Mental health|mental health]] patients would fare better in their families and communities. Historians Jansen and Osterhammel call him "the most influential anticolonial thinker of his time".

German football player and manager, nicknamed *der Kaiser* ("the Emperor"). Versatile, he started as a midfielder but made his name as a center-back and is often credited with inventing the modern sweeper, or libero. He appeared 103 times for [[West Germany]] in three [[FIFA World Cup|World Cups]] and two European Championships, and he captained the team to the 1974 World Cup title. He repeated the feat as a manager in 1990. At Bayern Munich he won three consecutive European Cups from 1974 to 1976, becoming the first player to win three European Cups as captain. He led Germany's successful bid to host the 2006 World Cup. In August 2024 the International Sports Press Association ranked him third-best footballer of the past 100 years, after [[Pelé]] and [[Diego Maradona]].

German-born American anthropologist and ethnomusicologist, often called the "Father of American Anthropology". Boas studied physics and geography in Germany, then conducted fieldwork among the [[Inuit]] of [[Baffin Island]] and in the [[Pacific Northwest]]. He emigrated to the United States in 1887 and in 1899 became professor of [[Anthropology|anthropology]] at [[Columbia University]]. His students included Ruth Benedict, Edward Sapir and [[Margaret Mead]]. Boas rejected evolutionary theories that ranked societies in stages, arguing that culture develops historically and is the central concept of anthropology. His studies showed that cranial shape was highly malleable depending on environmental factors such as health and nutrition, challenging scientific racism. He also helped create the four-field subdivision of anthropology, uniting [[Archaeology|archaeology]], physical anthropology, ethnology and [[Linguistics|linguistics]].

Habsburg emperor of Austria and king of Hungary (r. 1848–1916). He ascended the throne at eighteen after his uncle abdicated during the Hungarian Revolution of 1848, and he resisted constitutionalism in the early part of his reign. The Compromise of 1867 created the dual monarchy of [[Austria-Hungary]], granting Hungary greater autonomy. Tragedies marked his reign, including the execution of his brother [[Maximilian I of Mexico|Maximilian]] in 1867, the suicide of his son Rudolf in 1889 and the assassination of his wife in 1898. In 1914 the assassination of his nephew and heir, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, in [[Sarajevo]] led to [[World War I]].

German-language Jewish writer from [[Prague]]. His works fuse realism and the fantastic and typically feature isolated protagonists facing bizarre or incomprehensible bureaucratic powers. The term *Kafkaesque* describes situations like those in his writing. His best-known works include the novella *The Metamorphosis* (1915) and the novels *The Trial* (1925) and *The Castle* (1926). Trained as a lawyer, he worked in insurance and felt his true vocation was writing. Only a minority of his works were published in his lifetime. He died of [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]], relatively unknown. His literary executor, Max Brod, ignored Kafka's wish to destroy his remaining works and published them to eventual acclaim.
